title: The tree by the water (Psalm 1)
hookLine: the happy person is like a tree planted by rivers

lines: THE FRONT DOOR IS A TREE.
cards: Monks chant them in the dark before dawn. People whisper them at bedsides. A hundred and fifty poems: praise and complaint, thanks and rage, songs for a crowd and songs for one person awake at night.

The Psalms: a songbook, not a story. For fifty days, the path reads them and the wisdom books. And the very first psalm, the front door to the whole collection, opens with a picture: a tree, growing beside a stream.

teach.h: WALK, STAND, SIT: THE SLOW DRIFT.
teach.b: Psalm one begins, in the King James Bible: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful." Notice the slow drift.
Walking, then standing, then sitting. Passing bad advice, lingering, then pulling up a chair as a scoffer yourself. Nobody sits down all at once.
Blessed here is the Hebrew ashrei, which also means happy, or how fortunate: the book of praises opens with oh, the happiness of.
Then: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."

teach.h: HAGAH: MURMUR IT, LIKE A DOVE.
teach.b: Meditate, in Hebrew hagah, is a sound word, used elsewhere for a dove's moan and a lion's growl over its prey. To meditate on scripture was to murmur it under your breath, over and over, chewing on it.
And then the picture: "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither."
In a dry land, a tree beside an irrigation channel is a small miracle.
Its roots go down to water nobody sees. It still has seasons; it doesn't fruit all year. But it doesn't dry up in the heat.

teach.h: LIKE A TREE PLANTED BY THE RIVERS OF WATER.
teach.b: The psalm ends with the other kind of life, which it calls chaff, the husks that blow away on the threshing floor.
Two ways, the last verse says: the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly, right at the door of the book.
Saint Benedict's Rule for monks spreads all hundred and fifty psalms across each week, and some communities still keep that weekly round.

how: Christians pray the Psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, in the Anglican Daily Office and in personal devotions; some monastic communities pray the whole Psalter each week.

o: holy, set apart from everyday life
obedient, careful to keep every rule

games.q: what's inside Psalm 1 — tap the pairs.

s: the Psalms begin with a command
Psalm 1 opens with a blessing and a picture: a tree by the rivers of water.
the tree in Psalm 1 bears fruit all year
it bringeth forth his fruit in his season. its leaf doesn't wither.
in Hebrew, to meditate could mean to murmur
hagah is used for a dove's moan and a lion's growl.

games.q: the psalm describes someone drifting toward the scornful. what's the order?
games.why: walketh, standeth, sitteth: passing by, lingering, then settling in. nobody sits down all at once.

practice: Find a tree you can see from a window, or picture one you know, beside a creek or a canal or a fountain.
Imagine its roots reaching down toward water you can't see, and murmur one line under your breath, again and again: planted by the water. If you pray, ask where your roots are reaching.

wordCard.voice: Ashrei. Hebrew for blessed, happy, how fortunate, the first word of the Psalms: the life rooted like a tree by hidden water, fruit in its season.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessed, happy, how fortunate. The first word of the whole book of Psalms.

carryVoice: Your line: planted by the water. Seasons still come, but the leaf doesn't wither. A new block, begun.
